What it is: Paints, coatings and sheets that reflect sunlight, so less heat gets into the building.
Usually paid for by: Building owners, employers, housing programmes, and city or NGO schemes for low-income homes.
Things to check: Does the roof belong to the people who live there, or will the owner agree?; Who recoats or repairs it when it wears, and who pays?; Has the product been tested for how much sunlight it reflects?
Cycles it can help break: The cooling trap; The energy-poverty trap; The sleepless-nights loop; The poverty–heat trap
Research definition: Reflective roof products, installation, quality checks and recoating services intended to reduce solar heat gain.
Research note on reaching lowest-income: Subsidised/community retrofits can reach low-income occupants; roof control, rent and upkeep matter. No poorest-quintile reach verified.

What it is: Shading, insulation, false ceilings, ventilation and layouts that keep buildings cool with little or no power.
Usually paid for by: Developers, building owners, schools, clinics and public housing budgets.
Things to check: Is it designed for this climate, including humid weather and hot nights?; Will it work in existing homes, not only new buildings?; Who checks that it was built as designed?
Cycles it can help break: The sleepless-nights loop; The lost-schooling loop; The cooling trap; The energy-poverty trap; The displacement loop
Research definition: Shading, insulation, ventilation design, glazing, ceilings and heat-resilient retrofit/construction services; excludes roof coatings already assigned above.
Research note on reaching lowest-income: Public/social-housing procurement can provide access; informal tenure and permissions may prevent otherwise cheap works.

What it is: Shade structures, trees and planting in streets, markets, bus stops and schoolyards, and the care that keeps them alive.
Usually paid for by: Cities, market and transport managers, landowners and employers.
Things to check: Is there water and a paid caretaker for the dry season?; Could the improvement push up rents or move vendors out?; Is the shade where people actually wait, walk and work?
Cycles it can help break: The dying-green loop; The green-displacement loop; The cooling trap; The poverty–heat trap
Research definition: Shade structures, trees, green roofs/walls and planting/irrigation/maintenance services with a documented cooling purpose.
Research note on reaching lowest-income: Free public shade can benefit poor users; siting, accessible routes and anti-displacement measures determine reach.

What it is: Fans that move air using much less electricity, and the people who install and repair them.
Usually paid for by: Households, employers, and governments or utilities buying in bulk.
Things to check: Is it affordable to buy and to run?; Can it be repaired locally?; Fans help less in extreme heat: what else is in place on the hottest days?
Cycles it can help break: The energy-poverty trap; The sleepless-nights loop; The cooling trap; The global cooling loop
Research definition: Ceiling, table, pedestal and ventilation fans, including efficient motors, installation and repair.
Research note on reaching lowest-income: Lower upfront/running costs than some refrigerated systems can help, but no poorest-quintile affordability proof was established. Shared/public procurement can bridge access.

What it is: Coolers that use water to cool the air. They work well in dry heat, but much less well in humid heat.
Usually paid for by: Households, workshops and factories in dry climates.
Things to check: Is the air dry enough where it will be used?; Is there enough clean water, and who cleans the pads?; Could it make a humid room feel worse?
Cycles it can help break: The energy-poverty trap; The cooling trap; The energy–water loop
Research definition: Direct and indirect evaporative coolers, wet-media systems and their installation/cleaning services.
Research note on reaching lowest-income: Lower-cost models may improve access in suitable dry conditions; water and upkeep can still make them unaffordable.

What it is: Air conditioners that use less electricity, sized and installed correctly, and serviced regularly.
Usually paid for by: Households, building owners, employers and public institutions.
Things to check: Can the people using it afford the electricity?; What happens in a power cut?; Does it push heat into the street or next door?
Cycles it can help break: The cooling trap; The global cooling loop; The energy-poverty trap; The sleepless-nights loop; The overwhelmed-clinic loop
Research definition: Efficient inverter/split/window and packaged refrigeration-based cooling, installation, controls and repair; district systems are separate.
Research note on reaching lowest-income: Targeted subsidies or public cool rooms can help; tariffs, outages, tenure and installation barriers remain.

What it is: Trained technicians who service cooling equipment safely and collect old cooling gases (refrigerants), which warm the planet if they leak.
Usually paid for by: Equipment owners, manufacturers and public training programmes.
Things to check: Are the technicians trained and certified?; Where do the old gases go?; Is the gas used safe for this setting?
Cycles it can help break: The global cooling loop; The cooling trap
Research definition: Refrigerant supply, technician training, leak detection, safe maintenance, reclamation and end-of-life recovery for cooling equipment.
Research note on reaching lowest-income: Indirect reach through maintained affordable appliances; technician coverage and owner ability to pay determine access.

What it is: Central plants that cool many buildings through pipes, and companies that sell cooling as a service instead of selling machines.
Usually paid for by: Developers, building owners and large public buildings.
Things to check: Who can connect, and at what price?; Does it serve buildings people rely on in a heatwave?; What does the contract say if the service fails?
Cycles it can help break: The cooling trap; The global cooling loop; The energy–water loop
Research definition: Central chilled-water networks and long-term building cooling services, including storage when contracted within the cooling asset.
Research note on reaching lowest-income: Commercial-campus transactions do not demonstrate access for informal settlements; public anchor demand and tariff safeguards would need separate design.

Kind of protection: Cold storage for food and medicine
What it is: Cold rooms, milk chillers, fridges and transport that stop food and medicines spoiling in the heat.
Usually paid for by: Farmers’ groups, traders, food companies and health systems.
Things to check: Are there enough users nearby to keep it running?; Who sets the fees, and can small farmers afford them?; Is there backup power?
Cycles it can help break: The farm-debt loop; The heat credit squeeze; The overwhelmed-clinic loop; The energy–water loop
Research definition: Off-grid/weak-grid cold rooms, precooling, refrigerated transport and medical refrigeration with appropriate separate standards.
Research note on reaching lowest-income: Pay-per-use reduces equipment ownership barriers, but the poorest may lack produce volumes, transport or cash. Medical access normally requires institutional funding.

What it is: Cooling vests, shaded and cooled rest areas, and similar protection for people working in the heat.
Things to check: Do workers also get paid rest, not just equipment?; Is it practical for the real work?; Who cleans, recharges and replaces it?
Cycles it can help break: The poverty–heat trap; The overwhelmed-clinic loop
Research definition: Cooling garments, conductive/phase-change systems and portable cooled recovery services used as additions to environmental and work protection.
Research note on reaching lowest-income: Employer-paid provision can reach low-paid workers; self-purchase and unpaid recharge time exclude others.

What it is: Instruments that measure how hot a workplace, classroom or home really is, combining heat, humidity, sun and wind (often reported as WBGT, the wet-bulb globe temperature).
Usually paid for by: Employers, cities, schools and research programmes.
Things to check: What will people do when the reading is high?; Who checks the sensors are accurate?; Have workers agreed how the data is used?
Cycles it can help break: The invisible-deaths loop; The overwhelmed-clinic loop; The poverty–heat trap
Research definition: Instrument sales, rental, calibration, indoor monitoring and exposure dashboards tied to an actionable response.
Research note on reaching lowest-income: Institutional/collective purchase can cover informal or poor communities; retail wearable access is unverified.

What it is: Forecasts, alerts and risk maps that help people and organisations prepare for heat.
Usually paid for by: Businesses and insurers by subscription; public budgets for public warnings.
Things to check: Do warnings reach people without smartphones, in local languages?; Is there a plan for what happens after the alert?; Can the public see the data?
Cycles it can help break: The reactive-spending loop; The invisible-deaths loop; The poverty–heat trap; The heat credit squeeze
Research definition: Heat forecasts, risk analytics, APIs, local thresholds, translation and last-mile warning-to-action services, including heat analytics for lenders/cities.
Research note on reaching lowest-income: Public/local-language/offline distribution can reach poor users; subscription-only products and smartphone delivery are insufficient.

What it is: Insurance that pays out automatically when heat passes a set level, often to replace lost income. It is sometimes called parametric insurance.
Usually paid for by: Policyholders, employers, worker organisations, and premium support from governments or donors.
Things to check: Could someone lose income on a hot day and still get no payout?; Who pays the premium next year?; How fast is the money paid, and how?
Cycles it can help break: The protection-gap loop; The poverty–heat trap; The heat credit squeeze
Research definition: Insurance underwriting, distribution, triggers, claims/payment administration and independent assessment for heat-driven income losses.
Research note on reaching lowest-income: Group enrolment and premium support may help; current premium support and poorest-quintile reach were not verified for the cited example.

What it is: Loans, pay-as-you-go plans, repayment through the electricity bill, and group buying that spread the cost of cooling.
Usually paid for by: Borrowers and buyers, with lenders, utilities and sometimes subsidies.
Things to check: What is the total cost, including fees?; What happens after a missed payment?; Who can’t qualify, for example tenants or people without a bank account?
Cycles it can help break: The energy-poverty trap; The heat credit squeeze; The protection-gap loop
Research definition: Cooling-specific credit, leases, on-bill/PAYG contracts, bulk buying and guarantees enabling eligible cooling purchases; underlying equipment remains in its product segment.
Research note on reaching lowest-income: Unstable income, informal tenure and lack of meters can exclude the poorest even with smaller installments; assess disposable income and service continuity.

What it is: Safe drinking-water points, refills and reliable supply during heatwaves.
Usually paid for by: Cities, water utilities, employers, schools and clinics.
Things to check: Is the water free and safe to drink?; Does it keep working in a heatwave or power cut?; Are there toilets nearby?
Cycles it can help break: The energy–water loop; The overwhelmed-clinic loop; The poverty–heat trap
Research definition: Safe drinking-water refill, storage, filtration, maintenance and backup supply explicitly serving hot workplaces, clinics and public heat protection.
Research note on reaching lowest-income: Free safe points and accessible sanitation can help poor users; paid water can exclude them during the hottest hours.

What it is: Help for employers to assess heat risk, plan rest breaks, train staff and follow heat rules.
Usually paid for by: Employers, brands that buy from them, and labour departments.
Things to check: Do all workers, including contract workers, get paid rest?; Can workers raise concerns safely?; Who checks that the plan is followed?
Cycles it can help break: The poverty–heat trap; The overwhelmed-clinic loop; The protection-gap loop
Research definition: Risk assessment, work-rest protocols, training, inspection support, worker representation, schedule design and implementation assurance; devices are separate products.
Research note on reaching lowest-income: Reaches informal workers only if employers, buyers or public programmes cover them; ordinary compliance markets may miss them.

What it is: Seeds that cope with heat, and advice that helps farmers and farm workers through hot seasons.
Usually paid for by: Farmers and farmers’ groups, seed companies and agriculture departments.
Things to check: Can women farmers and tenant farmers get it?; Does it protect farm workers as well as crops?; Is local advice available?
Cycles it can help break: The farm-debt loop; The dry-soil loop; The poverty–heat trap
Research definition: Heat-tolerant seed, licensing/multiplication and heat-specific agronomic advice; farm fans, shade and storage retain their equipment segment.
Research note on reaching lowest-income: Public/community seed channels may reach low-income growers; landless workers may gain little without labour protection.

What it is: Training, cooling and equipment that keep clinics working in a heatwave and help staff treat heat illness early.
Things to check: Is the clinic itself cool enough for patients and staff?; Is care for heat illness free or affordable?; Who maintains the equipment after the first year?
Cycles it can help break: The overwhelmed-clinic loop; The invisible-deaths loop; The medical-debt trap; The reactive-spending loop
Research definition: Facility preparedness, emergency cooling procurement, staff training, surveillance support and continuity of care explicitly addressing heat.
Research note on reaching lowest-income: Public/free care and accessible outreach can reach poor people; private fee-for-service cooling/care may exclude them. No universal free-treatment entitlement inferred.

What it is: Controls, storage and backup that keep essential cooling running and ease pressure on the grid at peak times.
Usually paid for by: Utilities, building owners and facility managers.
Things to check: Are clinics, water pumps and shelters protected first in a power cut?; Who pays for backup that is rarely used?; Does it shift costs onto households?
Cycles it can help break: The energy–water loop; The cooling trap; The overwhelmed-clinic loop
Research definition: Cooling-specific demand response, controls, backup design and thermal/electrical storage integration; generic solar is excluded without a cooling use case.
Research note on reaching lowest-income: Most offers require controllable assets, meters and connectivity; poor households may be excluded or harmed by unsafe curtailment.
